lesson.menu_title: The Verbs That Run the Close
lesson.menu_desc: Look into it, hand it over, get back to you — the two-part verbs of every closing call -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 13 -- The Verbs That Run the Close
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Keitma Netto Cascarelli Gomes | Lesson 13 -- The Verbs That Run the Close

listenings.text: I run the monthly closing call for Latin America, and I have listened to a lot of updates. The ones I remember are short, and they move. Somebody says: I looked into the variance, I will get back to you by Thursday, and I would like to bring up one risk before we finish. That is three verbs in two parts, and I know exactly what happened, what comes next, and when. The updates I forget sound like a report being read out loud. An investigation was conducted, and a response will be provided in due course. It is correct English, and it is perfect for an email to the auditors. But in a call, it sounds like the person is hiding behind the sentence. So my advice is simple. Write like a report when you write to the auditors. Speak like a person when you speak to me.

I am an audit senior, and every year I visit about fifteen clients. By the second week, I know which ones will finish on time, and it is never about the size of the company. It is about the handover. The good teams put together a list of every working paper on day one, and they hand it over with the dates already filled in. When something is missing, they point it out before I find it. They say: this reconciliation is not ready, we are sorting it out, and you will have it on Wednesday. I have never complained about a team that told me first. The teams that worry me are the quiet ones. They do not bring anything up, and on the last day I discover three problems at once.
